introduction-the-big-bang-myth.core: Rewriting a legacy system from scratch in one go (big bang) usually fails: it freezes features, chases a moving target and loses hidden business rules. Incremental replacement is safer.

first_principles.problem: The 15-year-old monolith is tangled and scary, so the team proposes a full rewrite. Two years later the rewrite still isn't done, the old system kept changing, and undocumented behaviours are missing.
truths: Legacy code encodes years of hidden rules.
The business can't stop for years.
derivation: Don't stop the world; **replace piece by piece**.
Keep the old system **running and earning** during migration.
Prove each new piece in production before the next.

analogy.title: Rebuilding a bridge while traffic flows
analogy.story: You don't close the only bridge for two years. You build new lanes alongside and divert traffic lane by lane.
analogy.breaks: Bridges have fixed specs. Business requirements keep changing during a migration.

example.title: The two-year rewrite
example.scenario: A rewrite of a billing monolith.

steps.label: Hidden rules
steps.detail: Pro-rated refunds for one big customer existed only in old code.

example.outcome: you see why incremental migration is the default.

check.q: Why do big-bang rewrites chase a moving target?
check.a: The old system must keep changing for the business while the rewrite tries to catch up.

the-strangler-fig-analogy.core: Like the strangler fig tree that grows around a host and gradually replaces it, new services grow around the legacy system, taking over its functions until the old one can be removed.

first_principles.problem: We need a mental model for replacing a living system without killing the business that depends on it.
truths: The host keeps living while the fig grows.
derivation: Start **small**, attached to the old system.
Grow **around** it, taking over function by function.
When everything is replaced, **remove** the host.

analogy.title: The strangler fig tree
analogy.story: A seed lands in a host tree's canopy, sends roots down, gradually envelops the trunk, and after years stands on its own where the host once was.
analogy.breaks: The fig grows on its own. Migrations need sustained funding and attention, or they stall halfway.

example.title: Replacing a CMS
flow: New article pages served by new service

steps.label: Gradual
steps.detail: Each section moves only when ready.

example.outcome: the old system shrinks steadily while users see continuous service.

points: Grow around, not replace at once.
Remove the host at the end.

check.a: Martin Fowler, after the strangler fig trees he saw in Australia.

the-three-phases-of-strangler-fig-migrat.core: Strangler migrations run in three phases: intercept (put a proxy in front), replace (build new services for slices and route to them), and eliminate (remove the old code once unused).

first_principles.problem: Teams jump straight to building new services without a control point, then can't route traffic gradually or roll back.
truths: You need control over traffic before shifting it.
Slices must be replaced one at a time.
Old code must eventually be deleted.
derivation: **Intercept**: proxy passes 100% through unchanged; you gain a control point.
**Replace**: build a new service for one slice; route that slice to it.
**Eliminate**: delete the dead legacy code and data paths.

analogy.title: Renovating room by room
analogy.story: First install a hallway door you control (intercept), then renovate one room at a time (replace), then demolish the old wing (eliminate).
analogy.breaks: Rooms are separate. Legacy functions share data, which makes 'one slice at a time' harder.

example.title: Migrating user profiles

steps.label: Eliminate
steps.detail: Many teams forget this step and keep paying for both.

example.outcome: a disciplined path that keeps rollback possible at every step.

check.q: What does the intercept phase change for users?
check.a: Nothing: the proxy passes everything through; it just gives you a control point.

step-1-event-interception-the-proxy.core: Put an intercepting proxy (API gateway, facade) in front of the monolith so every request passes through a point you control. Then routing a path to a new service is a config change.

first_principles.problem: Clients and users talk directly to the monolith. To move functionality, you'd have to change every client. You need one place to redirect traffic.
truths: Path- or header-based routing can split traffic precisely.
derivation: Deploy a **proxy** (NGINX, Envoy, API gateway) in front.
Start with **100% passthrough**.
Add **rules** per path or feature to send traffic to new services.
Use it for **gradual percentages** and **instant rollback**.

analogy.title: A building receptionist
analogy.story: Every visitor checks in at reception before being directed. To move a department, the receptionist simply sends visitors to the new office.
analogy.breaks: Receptionists add little delay. A proxy adds a network hop and must be highly available.

example.title: Routing /api/users
example.scenario: Moving user endpoints to a new service.

steps.label: Config
steps.detail: One route block changes the destination.

code.text:
location /api/users/ { proxy_pass http://user-service; }
location /            { proxy_pass http://legacy-monolith; }

example.outcome: moving functionality becomes a reversible routing change.

check.q: Why start the proxy with 100% passthrough?
check.a: To prove the proxy itself is safe before any functional change.

choosing-what-to-strangle-first.core: Pick a first slice that is low-risk, loosely coupled, valuable enough to show progress, and well understood. Avoid starting with payments or auth.

first_principles.problem: A first slice that's too risky can break critical features and kill the project; one that's too trivial proves nothing and loses stakeholder support.
derivation: Score candidates on **business risk, coupling, value, clarity, data ownership**.
Prefer **read-heavy, edge** functions (e.g. notifications, catalogue display).
Avoid **payments, auth** first.
Use the first slice to **build the pipeline** (proxy, sync, monitoring).

analogy.title: Learning to swim
analogy.story: You start in the shallow end, not the deep end, but you do get in the water so you actually learn.
analogy.breaks: Pools have marked depths. Monolith coupling must be discovered by analysis.

example.title: Choosing among three slices
example.outcome: an early, safe win that proves the approach.

points: Low risk, low coupling, visible value.

check.a: It's critical and touches everything; a mistake breaks the whole product.

the-hardest-part-data-synchronization.core: Routing requests and rewriting logic is the easy part. The hard part is data: the new service needs its own data while the monolith still reads and joins on the same records.

first_principles.problem: You move user profiles to a new service with its own database, but the monolith's orders and reporting modules still join on the old users table. You can't just switch it off.
truths: Data is shared across many legacy modules.
derivation: Accept that data must exist in **both places** for a while.
Choose a sync strategy: **shared database**, **dual writes**, or **CDC**.
Decide which side is the **source of truth** at each phase.

analogy.title: Moving house with shared post
analogy.story: While you're moving, mail still arrives at the old address and family still use it. You need forwarding until everyone updates the new address.
analogy.breaks: Mail forwarding is one-way and simple. Data may change on both sides, which is much harder.

example.title: Users table used everywhere
example.scenario: Orders and reporting join on users.

steps.label: Reality
steps.detail: Turning off the old table would break three modules.

example.outcome: data sync is planned up front, not discovered mid-migration.

check.q: Why can't you just turn off the legacy table?
check.a: Other legacy modules still read and join on it.

data-sync-strategy-0-shared-database-tra.core: Simplest first step: the new service temporarily reads and writes the monolith's database. It breaks 'each service owns its data', which is fine for a while, because it splits extracting code from extracting data.

first_principles.problem: Doing code extraction and data migration at the same time doubles the risk.
truths: Temporary compromises need an end date.
derivation: **Step 1**: extract logic into a service using the **same database**.
**Step 2**: later, move the data to its own store.
Set a **deadline** so 'temporary' doesn't become permanent.

analogy.title: Moving out but keeping the old kitchen
analogy.story: You move into a new flat but still cook in the old one for a few weeks while the new kitchen is fitted.
analogy.breaks: Cooking in two places is obvious. A shared DB silently couples schema changes across teams.

example.title: Profile service on the legacy DB

steps.label: Benefit
steps.detail: Logic changes are tested without data risk.

example.outcome: two smaller, safer steps instead of one big one.

check.q: Why is sharing the DB acceptable here?
check.a: It's a temporary step that separates code risk from data risk.

data-sync-strategy-1-dual-writes.core: Dual writes make the application write to both old and new databases. It's simple to start but the two writes aren't atomic, so failures and races leave the copies inconsistent.

first_principles.problem: If the legacy write succeeds and the new write fails (or the order of concurrent writes differs), the stores diverge silently.
truths: Two separate writes can't be atomic without coordination.
derivation: Write to **both** in application code.
Add **retries and reconciliation** jobs to catch drift.
Compare stores regularly.
Prefer **CDC** when consistency matters.

analogy.title: Writing in two notebooks
analogy.story: You copy every note into two notebooks. Eventually you forget one, or write two notes in a different order.
analogy.breaks: Notebooks can be compared by eye. Databases need reconciliation jobs to detect drift.

example.title: Profile update half-fails
example.scenario: The new DB times out after the legacy update succeeds.

steps.label: Risk
steps.detail: Users see different names depending on which path served them.

example.outcome: you understand why dual writes need reconciliation or a better strategy.

check.q: What's the core flaw of dual writes?
check.a: The two writes aren't atomic, so one can succeed while the other fails.

data-sync-strategy-2-change-data-capture.core: With CDC, the application writes only to the legacy database as before, and a tool like Debezium reads the database's transaction log and streams every change to the new store, in order, with no app changes.

first_principles.problem: Dual writes are fragile and require changing legacy code. We want reliable, ordered sync without touching the monolith.
truths: Reading logs doesn't change app code.
derivation: Keep writes on **legacy only**.
Use **CDC** (Debezium/Kafka) to stream changes.
Consumers update the **new store**.
Later, **reverse the flow** when the new service becomes the source of truth.

analogy.title: Reading the shop's till roll
analogy.story: Instead of asking every cashier to note sales twice, you read the till roll, which already records every sale in order.
analogy.breaks: Till rolls are simple. CDC needs replication slots and monitoring, or it can fill the database's disk.

example.title: Syncing users to the new service
example.scenario: Legacy MySQL to a new Postgres.

steps.label: Lag
steps.detail: A few seconds of delay; acceptable for profiles.

example.outcome: reliable sync with zero changes to legacy code.

check.q: Why is CDC more reliable than dual writes?
check.a: It follows the committed transaction log, so every change is captured in order, without partial writes in app code.

step-2-3-traffic-shifting-and-strangling.core: Shift traffic gradually: shadow first (copy requests, compare responses, discard the new ones), then canary a small percentage, ramp up, flip the source of truth, and finally delete the legacy path.

first_principles.problem: Switching 100% of traffic in one go exposes every user to new bugs at once.
truths: Shadow traffic tests with real requests at zero user risk.
derivation: **Shadow**: mirror requests, compare outputs.
**Canary**: 1% → 5% → 25% → 100%, watching metrics.
**Flip** source of truth (reverse sync).
**Strangle**: delete legacy code and data.

analogy.title: Test-driving before switching cars
analogy.story: You drive the new car alongside the old one, then use it for short trips, then daily, then sell the old one.
analogy.breaks: Cars don't share fuel. Services share data, so the source-of-truth flip needs careful sequencing.

example.title: Moving search
example.scenario: Search moves to a new service.

steps.label: Shadow
steps.detail: Found 0.2% differences from a sorting edge case.

steps.label: Canary
steps.detail: Error rate unchanged at 5%, then ramp.

example.outcome: the switch happens with evidence at every step.

check.q: What does shadow mode give you?
check.a: Real-traffic comparison between old and new without affecting users.

anti-patterns-and-failure-modes.core: Strangler migrations fail in predictable ways: the eternal strangler that never finishes, a distributed monolith, a proxy that becomes a bottleneck, and ignoring data. Set completion criteria and timelines.

first_principles.problem: Two services get extracted, momentum dies, and the team now runs a monolith plus services plus a proxy: worse than before.
truths: Services that share a database are still coupled.
derivation: Avoid the **eternal strangler**: define the end state and a timeline.
Avoid a **distributed monolith**: separate data, not just code.
Keep the **proxy** thin and highly available.
Track **% of traffic / functionality migrated**.

analogy.title: A half-renovated house
analogy.story: New kitchen, old bathroom, scaffolding everywhere, and both old and new wiring to maintain. Worse to live in than before.
analogy.breaks: Builders get paid on completion. Internal migrations lose funding unless progress is tracked.

example.title: A migration stalled at 20%
example.scenario: Two years in, 80% of the monolith remains.

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: Either commit resources to finish, or consciously stop and simplify.

example.outcome: migrations either finish or are deliberately ended, not left half-done.

check.a: A migration that never completes, leaving you maintaining both old and new systems indefinitely.
